Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented
I put on loud music or TV
Being around people in authority or uniform

Threat.value: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

Negative Appraisals.value: The world is a dangerous place
People are not what they seem
I feel like I don't know myself anymore

issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: For a refugee trauma profile, comments on sexual violence are too trauma-specific and suggest a sexual assault formulation that is not otherwise supported by the threat, memory, or appraisal items. Nothing else in the profile indicates sexual trauma content, making this trigger hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Evaluation: Situations in which other people evaluate me / my appearance / my performance
issues.explanation: Avoiding situations where others evaluate appearance/performance fits social-evaluative shame concerns, but the rest of the profile centers on danger, distrust, intrusive sensory recall, and hypervigilance rather than evaluation-based threat. This strategy is not well linked to the active trigger/threat/appraisal pattern and is clinically out of place.

vignette: María, a 34-year-old Latin American woman married to Carlos, has been struggling with the aftermath of her traumatic experience as a refugee. Now working as a prison guard, María is often haunted by triggers that are deeply rooted in her past. The smell of alcohol and the sound of authority commands frequently bring back vivid memories of her time as a refugee, during which she was forced to flee under threatening circumstances. One particularly distressing incident occurred when the aroma of spilled alcohol at the prison triggered intense recollections of being trapped in a crowded, chaotic environment where people were drinking excessively out of desperation. These olfactory cues immediately transported María back to that harrowing time, and she found herself reacting with heightened fear and anxiety. The vivid auditory recall of shouts and threats from authority figures further compounded her distress. The experience was so overwhelming that she had to take a break, feeling emotionally drained as she relived those terrifying moments. Maria’s maladaptive strategies have developed over time in response to these triggers. She often finds herself ruminating on how the event could have been prevented, which leads her to feel increasingly helpless and overwhelmed. The constant need to avoid authority figures has become a significant part of her daily routine. When she hears commands from supervisors or sees people in uniform, María reacts as if she is once again in danger, even when there is no actual threat present. This heightened sense of fear causes her to seek out what she perceives as the safest seat available and put on loud music or turn up the TV volume to distract herself. Her belief that the world is a dangerous place has deepened over time. María feels that people are not what they seem, and this distrust manifests in her daily interactions at work. She finds it difficult to trust her colleagues and supervisors, which leads her to avoid them whenever possible. This avoidance has created a cycle of isolation and rumination on how the event could have been prevented. The vivid memories of her time as a refugee are always lurking just beneath the surface. These memories are so clear and detailed that when they return, María often hears sounds from that traumatic period in her head. The emotional intensity of these recollections is overwhelming, and she frequently needs to take breaks or use sensory distractions like loud music to cope with them. María’s negative appraisals have played a significant role in maintaining this cycle. She has come to believe that the world is inherently dangerous and unpredictable, which further exacerbates her fear responses to triggers such as authority commands and people in uniform. This belief system also affects how she processes memories; her heightened sense of danger makes each memory more vivid and distressing. The frequent false alarms María experiences have only reinforced her negative appraisals and made it harder for her to distinguish between real and perceived threats. Her startle response to unexpected movements is a constant reminder of the fear that she carries within her, making it nearly impossible to feel safe in any environment. As time has passed, María’s maladaptive strategies have become more entrenched. She believes that by avoiding authority figures and seeking out safe seating arrangements, she can prevent future threats from occurring. However, this avoidance only reinforces her negative beliefs about the world and makes her memories even more distressing when they inevitably return. What finally brought María to seek help was a series of occupational consequences. Her constant need for breaks and distractions at work began to impact her job performance, leading to conflicts with her supervisors. She realized that she could no longer function effectively in her role without addressing the underlying issues. María is most afraid of never feeling safe again, but she hopes that therapy can help her reclaim a sense of security and identity. Through this process, it has become clear that María’s trauma continues to profoundly affect her life. The cycle of triggers, maladaptive strategies, negative appraisals, and vivid memories keeps tightening around her, making each day an uphill battle. She is determined to break free from these patterns and regain a sense of control over her life.
